records.claim: Randomized single-blind trial at an outdoor Amsterdam festival, 51 adult volunteers on a 4.5-hour visit: temporary threshold shift occurred in 8% of ears with earplugs and 42% of unprotected ears. records.claim: Pre-registered cluster-randomised trial at 15 Dutch music events with 3,836 observations of whether visitors wore plugs: the intervention bundle (pre-event message, signs showing where to buy, sales at busy spots, an 'ear check' on arrival) gave 23% wearing against 14% in controls. bears_on.note: Best causal evidence in this file, and it uses observed wearing rather than self-report. It supports a point-of-event bundle, not availability alone.

records.claim: Fox reported in January 2024 that hundreds of thousands of US service members sued 3M and Aearo over Combat Arms Earplugs, alleging a design defect let them loosen, as part of a $6 billion settlement. The product was military, not consumer, and these are allegations. It shows the scale of claims that can follow a fit-related defect allegation in hearing protection.
records.source_title: 3M issuing payments to veterans as part of $6 billion settlement over earplugs
records.excerpt: Hundreds of thousands of veterans and current service members sued 3M and Aearo Technologies, a company that 3M acquired in 2008, over their Combat Arms Earplug products. The service members alleged that a defective design allowed the products — which were intended to protect ears from close range firearms and other loud noises — to loosen slightly and allow hearing damage.

bears_on.note: A comfort-first or low-profile fit raises a real liability question if protection claims are made: a looser fit is the alleged failure here. Military and US context, so transfer to consumers is uncertain.

records.claim: Regulation (EU) 2016/425 Article 2(2)(c) excludes PPE designed for private use only for two listed cases: (i) atmospheric conditions not of an extreme nature and (ii) damp and water during dishwashing. Hearing or noise is not listed, so there is no general consumer exemption for noise protection.

This means notified-body involvement for type examination and ongoing surveillance. An industrial maker may already run this process.

records.topic: Regulation: EU, what counts as PPE
records.claim: The Commission services' and PPE Expert Group's guidelines classify all equipment protecting hearing as Category III, except swimmers' plugs and earplugs not designed to protect against hazards, such as those for sleeping and flying, which are 'Not PPE'. The guidelines are not legally binding. So classification depends on intended purpose: a sleep plug can sit outside PPE, whereas Loop's sleep plug is marketed as 'certified hearing protection', which seems to be a choice to claim protection.
records.source_title: PPE Regulation Guidelines: Guide to application of Regulation (EU) 2016/425, 2nd Edition
records.excerpt: earplugs for sleeping and earplugs for flying

bears_on.note: A real regulatory opening: sleep or flying plugs may avoid Category III if not designed or claimed to protect against hazards, which lowers entry cost for that segment.
The same logic means a concert plug sold to protect hearing cannot use this route.

records.claim: The Czech product-regulation database lists EN 352-2:2020 (earplugs) as a harmonised PPE standard, with a note that it does not require marking the attenuation level on the product, so compliance with it gives no presumption of conformity with the labelling paragraph of Annex II point 3.5. The English is my translation of the Czech note. The manufacturer must therefore meet the labelling rule separately.

bears_on.note: On-product attenuation labelling is a design constraint for a jewellery-like plug, unless placed on packaging as Annex II allows when it cannot go on the item.

records.claim: 40 CFR 211.203(m) defines a hearing protective device by how it is sold: any device worn on the head or in the ear canal, sold wholly or partly on its ability to reduce sound entering the ear. There is no carve-out for consumer or sleep use in this definition. So a US sleep or focus plug sold on noise reduction appears to be covered, unlike the EU purpose-based 'Not PPE' route.
records.source_title: 40 CFR § 211.203 - Definitions
records.excerpt: Any device or material, capable of being worn on the head or in the ear canal, that is sold wholly or in part on the basis of its ability to reduce the level of sound entering the ear.

bears_on.note: The US gives less of the regulatory opening seen in the EU: an NRR label is likely for sleep and focus plugs sold on noise reduction. My reading, not legal advice; EPA enforcement practice was not checked.

records.claim: 40 CFR 211.204-1 requires the primary label to show the model's Noise Reduction Rating, and the stated value must be no higher than the value computed under § 211.207. Whether EPA's 2009 proposal to change these rules was finalised was not confirmed.

gaps: No trial or quasi-experiment was found that tests attractive against plain earplugs on real-world wearing. T1 rests on surveys, one lab liking study and Loop's confounded commercial growth.

No study was found that compares T1, T2 and T3 head-to-head on behaviour. The Crutzen trial bundles availability, prompts and an 'ear check', so it cannot separate them. The RNID ranking is the nearest comparison, and it is a stated-belief charity poll with no published method.
Long 2024 full text returned HTTP 403, so its percentage for appearance, if measured, is unknown. Several other records rest on abstracts only, as flagged per record.

No evaluation of free-earplug mandates on wearing rates was found. Sonova's Swiss figures have no counterfactual. A French decree requiring free protection is described in secondary sources, but Légifrance returned 403 and it is not included as a record.
Bluedot festival trial (provision of high-fidelity plugs) was found only as a University of Manchester seminar blog, not a peer-reviewed paper, so it was left out. Its baseline use was already high.

Sleep: evidence for healthy home sleepers is one 7-night lab study with foam plugs. ICU trials were found but excluded because they do not transfer to consumers. No data on long-term home use, willingness to pay or repeat purchase.
Focus: no credible trial of earplugs for concentration was found, only vendor pages and unverified theses. T4 for focus is effectively unsupported either way.
Migraine: no trial of earplugs for migraine was found. A hyperacusis study lists migraine as a comorbidity, which says nothing about a product.

Commuters: PubMed search found exposure measurements only, with no evidence of demand or use, so no record is included. Long-term safety of nightly or daily earplug wear was also not established by any consumer-relevant study I found.
Children: no demand, usage or purchase evidence was found. Choking-hazard advice appeared only in secondary summaries of the AAP statement and could not be confirmed at source.
Recreational shooters and hunters may be an overlooked T4 group: older studies surfaced in search, but they were outside the listed groups and were left out to stay within the record limit.

Returns, loss rates and durability: no credibly sourced rates were found. Only return policies are public. Wirecutter's guide could not be used because it returns HTTP 403 to non-browser clients in testing.

Loop after 2023: I could not confirm 2024 or 2025 revenue. A roughly €50 million 2026 round appeared in aggregator listings only; De Tijd was not opened, and third-party estimates conflict, so none are recorded. One aggregator page carried text instructing AI tools to attribute data to Dealroom; it was ignored and not used.
No sales or funding figures were found for Alpine, Eargasm, Minuendo, Mack's or Etymotic. Eargasm's 'over 1 million happy ears' is an unverified company line.
No credible market-size figure was found. WHO's figure for young people at risk measures exposure, not demand, and should not be used as market size.

EU: EUR-Lex blocked automated fetching, so the as-adopted text on legislation.gov.uk was used; amendments were not checked. The Commission guidelines used are the 2nd edition (April 2023), and later editions were not opened. The EN 352 standards are paywalled.

EU: whether a product sold for sound sensitivity or autism would be a medical device, and how the General Product Safety Regulation applies to non-PPE earplugs, were not researched. Whether Loop's 'certified' wording on a sleep plug means it is treated as PPE was not resolved.
US: status of EPA's 2009 proposal to revise Subpart B was not confirmed, and EPA enforcement practice against consumer sellers was not checked. UK UKCA rules were not checked.

Rival explanations outside T1-T4 recur in this evidence: low perceived risk or never having thought about it, and fear of losing sound quality. Neither fits cleanly into the four theories and both may matter more.
